canonical_statement: The review evaluates what the authors consider to be successful, problematic, and emerging aspects of pulmonary embolism prevention and treatment.
The authors argue that pulmonary embolism care should incorporate anticoagulant pharmacokinetics rather than rely mainly on convenient historical dosing protocols.
The authors report increasing inpatient awareness, measurement, and quality-improvement activity around pulmonary embolism and deep-vein thrombosis prophylaxis.
In a cited Chinese hospital survey of patients with thromboembolism within 6 weeks after hospitalization, 31% received any prophylaxis.

population.label: Patients in surveyed Chinese hospitals with thromboembolism within 6 weeks after hospitalization, 2016-2017

canonical_statement: In the same cited Chinese survey, 5% of medical patients received prophylaxis classified as appropriate.

canonical_statement: In the same cited Chinese survey, 8% of surgical patients received prophylaxis classified as appropriate.

canonical_statement: The review describes broader multidisciplinary attention to pulmonary embolism across emergency medicine, cardiology, radiology, hematology, pharmacy, pulmonary medicine, and critical care.
The authors view protocolized pulmonary embolism treatment as potentially useful for standardization but caution that rigid protocols can impede individualized expert care.

The review notes newer CTEPH diagnostic thresholds of mean pulmonary artery pressure 20 mm Hg and pulmonary vascular resistance 2.0 Wood units, which the authors say will classify more patients as CTEPH.
The review identifies continuous intravenous LMWH, factor XI/XIa inhibition, novel fibrinolytic strategies, suction thrombectomy, and catheter-based techniques as areas of active development.
The authors argue that mandatory risk-score algorithms for inpatient VTE prophylaxis can complicate care and prefer prophylaxis unless contraindicated in many hospitalized patients.
The authors argue that pulmonary embolism response teams may be useful where PE expertise is limited but can delay or overcomplicate care where experienced consultants are already available.
The review states that earlier UFH studies associated more rapid attainment of the therapeutic aPTT threshold with fewer recurrent thromboembolic events.
The review gives a commonly cited prophylactic LMWH peak anti-Xa target range of 0.20-0.40 U/mL approximately 4 hours after subcutaneous injection.

The authors conclude that fixed once-daily subcutaneous LMWH prophylaxis can leave prolonged periods of low anticoagulant exposure and can underdose heavier patients while increasing exposure in leaner patients.
A cited perioperative enoxaparin study reported 3-5 hour anti-Xa peaks ranging from 0.10 to 0.55 U/mL after a 40 mg dose, with the lowest levels in the highest-weight patients.
For a cited fixed-dose LMWH regimen, the review reports a peak anti-Xa level of 0.28 U/mL in a 50 kg patient.
For the same cited fixed-dose LMWH regimen, the review reports a peak anti-Xa level of 0.13 U/mL in a 104 kg patient.
With weight-based LMWH at 50 U/kg in the cited report, peak anti-Xa activity was 0.18 U/mL in a 55 kg patient.
With weight-based LMWH at 50 U/kg in the cited report, peak anti-Xa activity was 0.20 U/mL in a 90 kg patient.
In cited healthy-volunteer data, mean anti-Xa after tinzaparin 75 U/kg once daily fell below 0.10 U/mL by 10 hours in normal-weight participants.

canonical_statement: In the same cited tinzaparin data, mean anti-Xa fell below 0.10 U/mL by 13 hours in heavy-weight participants.

In ICU patients not receiving vasopressors, the cited study reported a 4-hour mean anti-Xa level of 0.26 U/mL, with 16% below 0.14 U/mL.
In a cited Belgian ICU randomized study, the subcutaneous group had a mean peak anti-Xa level of 0.20 U/mL at 4 hours and 16% had levels of 0.10 U/mL or lower.

canonical_statement: The authors argue that wide interpatient anti-Xa variability in high-risk and ICU populations supports weight adjustment and more frequent or continuous dosing rather than reliance on group averages.

The review reports a trauma prophylaxis approach of enoxaparin 30 mg every 12 hours for 50-60 kg, 40 mg every 12 hours for 61-99 kg, and 50 mg every 12 hours for at least 100 kg, with peak anti-Xa targeting 0.2-0.4 U/mL.
The review notes that in a cited PE trial of once-daily weight-based tinzaparin versus UFH, 50% of tinzaparin patients had received at least 18 hours of intravenous UFH first.

canonical_statement: A cited 1983 hip-replacement study found adjusted subcutaneous UFH targeting an aPTT of 31.5-36 seconds more effective than fixed dosing without increased bleeding.

canonical_statement: For acute pulmonary embolism, the authors recommend rapidly monitored intravenous anticoagulation initially and continued intravenous therapy for most hospitalized patients until true hemodynamic stability and adequate perfusion are restored.

The authors state that a fully stable patient without hemodynamic or right-ventricular compromise can be transitioned from intravenous anticoagulation to subcutaneous LMWH or an approved direct oral anticoagulant.
The review describes ongoing investigation of weight-based intravenous LMWH prophylaxis with anti-Xa monitoring in critically ill patients.
The authors state that marked renal insufficiency warrants either a reduced LMWH dose or use of UFH for acute PE treatment.
The review describes suction thrombectomy as sequential pulmonary-artery catheter aspiration with filtration and reinfusion of blood, with approximately 60 minutes of total intervention.

A cited randomized catheter-directed thrombolysis trial used catheters for about 14 hours and an average total alteplase dose of 20 mg in each group; thrombus-score reduction was similar and no superiority was shown.

The authors argue that advanced-therapy trials using unmonitored subcutaneous LMWH control arms may not determine whether thrombectomy or catheter-directed lysis is superior to adequately delivered anticoagulation.
The review cites brain-imaging data reporting silent brain microbleeds in 20% of apparently healthy people older than 60 years and 33% of those older than 80 years.
The review describes alpha-2-antiplasmin inhibition as an investigational fibrinolytic strategy intended to promote clot lysis while potentially reducing distant bleeding.
The review describes factor XI/XIa inhibitors as investigational anticoagulants intended to reduce bleeding, while noting uncertainty about efficacy without conventional anticoagulation.
The review reports chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension after a first symptomatic PE as relatively rare, about 4% at 2 years.

population.label: Patients after a first symptomatic pulmonary embolism

canonical_statement: The review states that supportive evidence is not available for benefit from adhering to detailed post-PE sporting-activity regimens described in a consensus follow-up document.

The authors conclude that PE prevention and treatment would benefit from greater incorporation of pharmacokinetic evidence and from clinical trials designed to have explanatory power and practice-changing integrity.
The authors report no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have influenced the work.
